answer:
VIABILITY: The model has a credible path to revenue, and early evidence supports it. Four paying pilots ($41.5K collected, ~$12K spent) and two stated intents to sign annual packages show real willingness to pay, which is rare at this stage. Pricing ($18K standard, $9.5K light, $2.5K add-ons) is sensible for the segment and sits well below the $50K+ consulting alternative, and two-installment payments help cash flow. The service is clearly differentiated by closing the loop from data to lesson plans to remeasured growth. However, viability is not yet proven: pilot pricing and scope are unclear (average pilot revenue is ~$10.4K, roughly half the target package), 'intends to sign' is not a signed contract, and renewal is the core economic driver but untested. 'Profitable on paper' ignores unpaid founder labor; with realistic coach and founder compensation, margins are likely much thinner than the stated 60% gross margin.

SCALABILITY: This is the weakest area. The model is a human-delivered service: each school gets 9 coaching workshops plus 3 findings briefs per year, and coach time is the main cost. Revenue scales roughly linearly with headcount, so reaching 60 schools implies ~540 workshops, 180 briefs and substantial travel, which means a bench of many trained coaches rather than 2 part-timers. Quality control, coach recruiting/retention, and school-calendar seasonality (everyone wants support right after the same testing windows) will strain delivery. The claim that margins will rise as templates and the dashboard cut prep time is plausible but unquantified; the human coaching session, which is the differentiator, cannot be automated away without losing the value proposition. Growth is therefore more likely to follow a good services-business curve than a software curve.

ASSUMPTIONS: (1) TAM math is simplistic: 3,500 schools x $18K = $63M assumes every target school will buy a full package, ignoring budget constraints, school closures/turnover, and that many small charters spend far less than $18K on data support. The $63M figure is a ceiling, not a market estimate. The 8,000-school and 3,500-fit figures are unsourced. (2) Sales cycle and CAC are ignored. Schools buy on academic-year budgets, decisions are slow, and 'talked to 30 of 140 schools' is interest, not pipeline. Going from 4 pilots to 12 full-price schools (3x) and then to 30 and 60 is aggressive with a student, part-time team whose CEO is also a full-time senior. (3) The 'word of mouth spreads fast' claim is plausible in a tight community but also cuts both ways if early results disappoint. (4) The projections have no stated cost build: no coach pay, travel, insurance, or founder salary assumptions, so the 'break even on hiring by mid year two' claim cannot be verified. (5) Impact is the product, yet there is no evidence yet that students actually improved. Pilot growth data, even small, is the single most important missing proof point and the basis for renewals and charter-renewal-driven urgency. (6) Competitive defensibility is thin: the approach is replicable by a larger firm or a software vendor adding a services layer, and templates are copyable. The real moat would be outcomes data, relationships, and a trained coach network, none of which exist at scale yet. (7) Data-privacy compliance (FERPA, student data agreements) is not mentioned and becomes a real operational burden when handling assessment exports.

STRATEGIC RECOMMENDATIONS: Convert pilots to signed annual contracts and report actual growth results; build a bottom-up cost and capacity model (schools per coach per year) to test margin and hiring plans; consider a hybrid or train-the-trainer tier (coaching school staff to run cycles themselves, or recorded/virtual coaching) to decouple growth from headcount; sequence geographically by clustering schools in the home state to cut travel; and lean on associations as a low-CAC channel.

VERDICT: A promising, early-validated, but capacity-limited services business. The path to making money is clear and near-term; the path to scaling is plausible only with disciplined unit economics, retained customers, and a delivery model that reduces dependence on founder and coach hours. Overall viability: moderate-to-good; scalability: moderate-to-low as currently designed; assumption rigor: moderate, with market sizing and growth projections the most optimistic elements.
